beats.narration_text: Salaam. This is Liam, in for Bear. It's tempting to ask how a compiler turns your code into a program in one go. But it doesn't happen in one go. So the real question is what a compiler does at each stage.

beats.narration_text: A compiler: a program that turns source code into a program a chip can run. A token: one word of code, like a name, a number, or a symbol. I R: the compiler's own in-between language. And assembly: a chip's instructions, written as text.

terms.meaning: turns source code into a program a chip can run
one word of code: a name, a number, a symbol
a chip's instructions, written as text

beats.narration_text: A compiler turns code written in C into a program a chip can run. Claude's C Compiler, which its read me says Claude wrote in Rust, from scratch, does it as one pipeline, with no outside tools. Let's follow one file through every stage.

shot.visual_intent: A white source page ('C source') waits at the left of a long pale belt; four machines rise onto the belt (three kraft, the last one dark with four lamps); the page rides through them in turn and comes out at the far end as a kraft box taped shut ('ELF program').
shot.motion_claim: A white source page ('C source') waits at the left of a long pale belt; four machines rise onto the belt (three kraft, the last one dark with four lamps); the page rides through them in turn and comes out at the far end as a kraft box taped shut ('ELF program').

beats.narration_text: First, the preprocessor. It works on the raw text: it pastes in each header named by a hash include, expands every macro, and drops any code that an if def switches off.

shot.visual_intent: The source page grows large ('preprocessor'); a header page slides in and merges at its top ('#include'); one line with a kraft macro tag widens into three lines ('macro'); a bracketed block of two lines fades out and the page closes up.
shot.motion_claim: The source page grows large ('preprocessor'); a header page slides in and merges at its top ('#include'); one line with a kraft macro tag widens into three lines ('macro'); a bracketed block of two lines fades out and the page closes up.

beats.narration_text: Next, the lexer chops that text into tokens. Each name, number and symbol becomes one tile, and every tile keeps its span: where in the file it came from.

shot.visual_intent: One line of the page lifts out and stretches into a long white strip ('lexer'); a terracotta scan line sweeps along it and the strip splits into kraft tiles of different widths ('tokens'); a small grey span tab drops under each tile, with a grey thread back to the page.

beats.narration_text: The parser reads the tokens in order and builds a syntax tree, which shows how the pieces fit together. It works by recursive descent: each grammar rule calls the rules for the parts inside it.

shot.visual_intent: The tiles rise one by one, left to right, and settle as the leaves of a tree; grey edges draw up to kraft branch nodes and a root ('syntax tree', 'parser'); the root lights, then each branch in turn, top down.

show.event: each rule calls the rules inside it

shot.motion_claim: The tiles rise one by one, left to right, and settle as the leaves of a tree; grey edges draw up to kraft branch nodes and a root ('syntax tree', 'parser'); the root lights, then each branch in turn, top down.

beats.narration_text: Then semantic analysis checks that the tree makes sense. It works out the type of every expression, computes constant values ahead of time, and records each name in a symbol table.

shot.visual_intent: Grey type tabs stamp onto the tree's nodes one by one ('types'); a small subtree folds up into a single node with a terracotta dot (a constant computed); a grey-outlined card at the right fills with rows as the name leaves send copies ('symbol table').

show.event: names go into the symbol table

beats.narration_text: Lowering turns the checked tree into I R, an in-between language that's the same for every chip. At first, every local variable gets a stack slot: its own box in memory.

shot.visual_intent: The tree shrinks away to the left and a column of white IR strips drops in, one by one ('IR'); below them a row of small open kraft boxes appears ('stack slots'), and a grey thread ties each variable strip to its box.

beats.narration_text: A pass called mem to reg then promotes those slots into registers. The result is S S A form, and where two paths through the code meet, a phi node picks which value arrives.

shot.visual_intent: The threads cut and the stack-slot boxes sink away; a dark register tab snaps onto each strip ('registers'); the column splits into two short paths that rejoin at one strip, where a terracotta dot lands ('phi node').

beats.narration_text: Now the optimizer runs a chain of passes over the I R, looping up to three times. Constant folding does the math it can already see, and dead code elimination deletes what nothing uses. Last, phi nodes become plain register copies.

shot.visual_intent: A grey loop track draws around the IR column with three round markers ('up to 3 rounds'); two strips merge into one (folding); two strips fade out and the column closes up (dead code); the terracotta phi dot turns into a plain grey strip ('optimizer').

beats.narration_text: Then the back end. The same I R can go to one of four chips: x eighty-six sixty-four, i six eighty-six, A. Arch sixty-four, or risk five sixty-four. The chosen code generator writes assembly for that chip.

beats.narration_text: Each back end then runs a peephole optimizer over its assembly. It finds wasted patterns, like storing a value and loading it straight back, and cuts the waste.

beats.narration_text: The built-in assembler turns that text into machine code. It parses each line, encodes each instruction as bytes, and writes an object file, a dot o.

shot.visual_intent: The strips ride into a kraft press ('assembler'); out the other side comes a row of grey byte tiles, one group per strip; the tiles pack into a kraft block ('.o file').

beats.narration_text: Last, the built-in linker. It reads the object file with the C runtime and libraries, resolves every symbol, finding where each named function lives, patches the code to point there, and writes the finished ELF executable.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. In Claude Code, paste this. Write add dot c, a main that sets x to two and y to three and returns x plus y. Using the C compiler on this machine, show it to me one stage at a time: the preprocessed text, the tokens, the syntax tree, and the assembly at O zero and at O two. Name the stage that made each one. Then build it and run it. Then check: does echo dollar question mark print five? And at O two, is the add instruction gone, folded into a five?

props.command: Write add.c, a main that sets x to 2 and y to 3 and returns x + y. Using the C compiler on this machine, show it to me one stage at a time: the preprocessed text, the tokens, the syntax tree, and the assembly at -O0 and at -O2. Name the stage that made each one. Then build it and run it.
output: Check: at -O2, is the add gone?
